findings.angle: A: Latvian law, permits, fire rules, penalties, producer registration and used-vs-waste battery shipments (research date 31 Oct 2026)
findings.summary: A hub can start with a State Environmental Service (VVD) waste management permit under Cabinet Regulation 703. State fees are EUR 120 per activity, EUR 180 for two and EUR 240 for three or more, so permit cost is not the barrier. No fixed issuing deadline exists in Reg 703. The larger risks are as follows. (1) Hazardous-waste storage above 50 t, or over a year, is a category B pollution permit; I found no clear lithium-battery shredding line in Annex 1 and could not confirm B-permit timing. (2) Reg 238 (fire) has no lithium-specific clause in the 200k of 246k characters I read, and likumi.lv says it loses force on 2 Jan 2027 with no successor found. (3) A pack only counts as 'used' for shipment if the full Annex XIV evidence file exists; a state-of-health test record alone is not enough, and missing evidence means waste and a presumed illegal shipment. (4) Fines are modest (about EUR 70 to 4,000) next to the cost of a fire. Several answers remain unverified, listed per item and in searched_not_found. Language coverage: Latvian, English, Estonian and German-language mirrors. I did not run Lithuanian, Swedish, Norwegian or Finnish searches that produced usable results.

items.question: Q1. Which waste permit or registration does a hub need to collect, store, sort and discharge used EV lithium traction batteries; who issues it; how long; what does it cost?
items.answer: Waste Management Law s.12(1) (likumi.lv): before collecting, transporting, transshipping, sorting or storing waste, an operator must obtain a VVD permit. Exemptions (s.12(6)): retail collection points for household waste; battery collection points under Reg (EU) 2023/1542; a holder's short-term storage of its own waste. These do not cover a commercial EV-pack hub that takes packs from third parties (my reading, estimate). Cabinet Reg 703 (13.09.2011, amended by Reg 729 of 09.12.2025) point 2: if an A or B category pollution permit already contains collection/sorting/storage conditions, no separate waste permit is needed. State fee (Reg 703 pt 21-23): EUR 120 per activity, EUR 180 for two, EUR 240 for three or more; EUR 70 for an amendment; EUR 100 for trader/intermediary registration. Application (pt 4) must list storage sites, storage types and annual tonnes, and signed contracts with recipients; pt 25 requires the recipient to hold the right permit. Timing: Reg 703 sets no fixed deadline for a new permit (amendment decisions 10 working days; trader registration 1 month). Classification (Reg 302): 16 06 05 'other batteries and accumulators' is listed non-hazardous; 16 06 01/02/03 and 16 06 06 are hazardous. So an intact Li-ion pack coded 16 06 05 is non-hazardous on paper, which may keep a small hub out of the hazardous-waste B-category thresholds; this is my inference and must be confirmed with VVD, particularly for damaged packs. Issuer: Valsts vides dienests (VVD).

items.question: Q2. Is a mechanical dismantling and shredding line subject to a different or higher permit category; what are storage limits and site requirements?
items.answer: Pollution Law Annex 1 (B category) lists: 5.14 shredding of electrical and electronic waste up to 75 t/day; 5.9 shredding of end-of-life vehicles up to 75 t/day; 5.5.4 recovery of non-hazardous waste including shredding of metal waste (item 5.5 capacity up to 75 t/day); 5.12 hazardous waste storage (outside place of generation) longer than one year; 5.13 hazardous waste storage up to one year, total capacity up to 50 t; 5.1 hazardous waste disposal/recovery up to 10 t/day; 5.10 non-hazardous waste sorting/storage/recovery where 30 t/day or more may be present. So a shredding line is B category (a pollution permit) not just a waste-management permit, and a B permit absorbs the Reg 703 permit (Reg 703 pt 2). Annex 2 (C, registration only, VVD checks within 14 days, notify 30 days beforehand) has no battery, hazardous-waste or metal-shredding item. Annex 1 (first 100,000 characters) names no lithium-battery recycling or black-mass line; whether a battery-pack shredder falls under 5.14, 5.1 or A category could not be determined (not found). Above-threshold A-category rules were not retrieved. Site requirements for battery storage and treatment (Cabinet Reg 485 of 2011, English consolidated text to 2014, pt 19-22): impermeable pollutant-proof covering or container; weatherproof cover; surface-water collection and oil traps where oils may escape; treatment sites also need scales, impermeable surface with drainage, place for dismantled parts, wastewater treatment, and separation of all fluids including acids; VVD regional board inspects treatment facilities at least once a year. Caveat: I could not confirm Reg 485 is still in force in this form in 2026 (one search hit says a related 2015 battery regulation lost force 12.12.2025).

items.question: Q3. What do Latvian fire rules say about storing lithium-ion batteries (Reg 238, LBN 201-10, VUGD guidance, insurer requirements)?
items.answer: No lithium-specific storage clause found. Cabinet Reg 238 of 19.04.2016 (Fire Safety Regulations; latest amendment seen Reg 381 of 25.06.2025; likumi.lv page states it loses force on 2 January 2027, successor not found). In the first 200,000 of 246,196 characters of the Latvian text I found only general or lead/alkali-battery rules: cl.24 and 38 (store substances according to physical and chemical properties); cl.62.7 (no combustibles in electrical rooms); cl.9 and 180.1.5 (stay within the maximum fire load set in the fire safety instructions); cl.296-297 (electric forklifts charged and stored in a fire-separated room with mechanical ventilation, separate power feed); cl.458-463 (charging rooms: own ventilation not connected to general ventilation, automatic cut-off if ventilation stops, no battery repair in the charging room; alkaline and acid batteries charged and stored in separate premises); cl.261 (at least 50% of extinguishers suitable for electrical equipment). The last 46,196 characters were not read, so a lithium clause there is not excluded. Building norm: the current one is LBN 201-15 (Cabinet Reg 333 of 30.06.2015; text in force as of 01.01.2026); I did not find LBN 201-10 in force (it appears superseded; my inference). Fire-compartment maximum sizes are in its Table 3, not retrieved; warehouse fire load must be stated in the fire safety measures report (pt 72.5.1). Amendments to Reg 333 had public consultation 7-21 Aug 2025; adoption status unknown. VUGD data: 39 fires linked to battery/accumulator burning in 2025 (20 short circuit, 11 damaged device); VUGD advice is to hand damaged lithium batteries to special collection points. Insurer requirements: not found (no Latvian insurer standard located; searched). Practical consequence (estimate): design the building to the general rules plus a fire-risk assessment and insurer survey before signing a lease; budget for fire-compartment separation, detection and a water/containment plan.

items.question: Q4. What penalties apply to waste handlers and battery producers who do not comply? Give euro ranges.
items.answer: Waste Management Law Chapter IX, Article 43 sets fines in fine units; one unit is EUR 5 under Administrative Liability Law Art.16(2) (Sorainen and LV Portals explanations; VVD's 2021 statement of EUR 1,000 natural / EUR 2,800 legal for a 200/560-unit offence matches this). Converted by me (estimate = units x 5): 43(6) collecting, transporting, sorting or storing without a permit: 14-200 units natural = EUR 70-1,000; 50-560 units legal = EUR 250-2,800. 43(2) breach of waste management rules: same ranges (a warning is also possible for natural persons). 43(3) breach of waste accounting rules: legal persons 50-250 units = EUR 250-1,250. 43(4) not using mandatory EEE/battery marking: legal persons 50-350 units = EUR 250-1,750. 43(5) battery/EEE producer failing to register: legal persons 50-350 units = EUR 250-1,750. 43(7) breach of cross-border shipment rules: natural 50-220 units = EUR 250-1,100; legal 60-800 units = EUR 300-4,000. Enforcer: VVD (Art.44). Not found: Natural Resources Tax rates for batteries, and any EPR-specific fine; the fines for an illegal shipment under Reg 1013/2006 and any criminal liability were not researched. The cost of a fire or a revoked permit will exceed these fines.

items.question: Q5. Producer registration and reporting duties for batteries in Latvia; must a repurposer or collector register?
items.answer: Cabinet Reg 331 of 17.06.2014 (in force; version from 1 May 2026, latest amendment Reg 227 of 28.04.2026) covers the register of EEE and battery producers under the Waste Management Law s.24 and 31. Register holder: Latvian Electrotechnical and Electronics Industry Association; controller: Ministry of Climate and Energy. Battery producers and authorised representatives under Reg (EU) 2023/1542 Art.56(3) must register before offering batteries on the Latvian market (cl.22), with proof of prepayment; foreign producers' authorised representatives register within one month of appointment (cl.23); foreign producers registered before 18 Aug 2025 had to appoint a representative by 15 June 2026 (cl.41.11). Registrar decision within 10 working days; changes and cessation notified within 10 working days. Annual data-maintenance fee: EUR 42.69 at registration and EUR 42.69 per calendar year, invoiced by 1 Feb and due by 28 Feb. Reg 331 sets no separate registration duty for collectors, repurposers or recyclers; a waste manager can submit collected-quantity and treatment data for a producer if it has a contract (cl.32). A waste manager's own duty is the permit (Q1) plus waste accounting (Art.43(3) fine). Whether a repurposer that sells a repurposed pack becomes a 'producer' under Reg 2023/1542 (it may if it places it on the market as new) was not verified in the fetched text; confirm with the Ministry of Climate and Energy before any resale. Old annual battery reporting date (20 April, Reg 789) is repealed text; the current date was not found.

items.question: Q6. Does a pack with a state-of-health test record count as 'used' and move across borders without waste-shipment paperwork (Reg 2023/1542, Waste Shipment Regulation, DIWASS)? Latvian authority contact?
items.answer: Not by the test record alone. Reg (EU) 2023/1542 Art.72(2) (note: the shipment article is 72; Art.73 covers preparing for re-use/repurposing) lets competent authorities check shipments of used batteries likely to be waste against the minimum requirements in Annex XIV. Annex XIV (via gesetze.legal, summary; verify against EUR-Lex): for each shipment the holder must keep (1a) invoice plus sale/transfer contract showing direct reuse and full functionality; (1b) per-battery assessment or test records (e.g. test certificate); (1c) a holder's declaration that nothing in the load is waste under Directive 2008/98/EC; (1d) adequate protection during transport and loading; (3) a test record (age/state of health and hazardous-substance check) attached to the battery or packaging with designation, ID number, year, tester name and address, test type, results and date; (4) a transport document and a declaration of responsibility for each load. Exemptions (point 2) exist for warranty returns to the manufacturer and some contracted repair or failure analysis under inter-company agreements. If any evidence is missing, the items are treated as waste and the shipment is presumed illegal under Arts 24-25 of Reg 1013/2006 (Annex XIV point 5). Art.73(1) separately lists evidence to show a prepared battery is no longer waste: state-of-health test records from a Member State, invoice/contract, transport protection. So a tested pack with a full Annex XIV file ships as a product (no waste paperwork); a pack taken back as end-of-life, the shredded fractions and black mass ship as waste under Reg 1013/2006 (notification or Annex VII, depending on the code), and Art.72(3) says exported waste counts to targets only with proof of equivalent treatment. Black mass shipment classification (green list vs notification) was not retrieved: not found. DIWASS: use is mandatory from 21 May 2026 for waste shipments (Reg 2024/1157; Andersen summary). Latvian competent authority: Valsts vides dienests, DIWASS code LV01 (Czech ministry list of 01.06.2026). Contact seen in VVD guidance: ap@vvd.gov.lv; the VVD 'Vides SOS' number +371 26338800 is for violation reports only, not shipments. VVD guidance lists a state fee of EUR 142.29 for the notification procedure (undated PDF, item 5, unverified).

findings.angle: B: what producers pay for take-back (PRO fee tables) and what recyclers charge or pay (gate fees, black mass payables), plus freight and tenders
findings.summary: Verified primary tariffs. (1) The cleanest real price for handing a pack to a recycler is GRS Service GmbH's price list valid 1 Jan 2026 (Germany): undamaged NMC/NCA modules cost the sender EUR 1.31/kg, plus EUR 214.50 for the first pallet slot (EUR 125 for each further slot). LFP costs EUR 3.68/kg. Damaged but transport-safe NMC modules cost EUR 1.44/kg plus EUR 236.50 per first pallet slot. Damaged and transport-critical NMC modules cost EUR 3.06/kg plus EUR 825 per safety container. So a 400 kg undamaged NMC pack costs about EUR 740 (EUR 1.85/kg all-in on one pallet). All prices exclude VAT. (2) Producer fees paid to compliance schemes for EV batteries vary about 25-fold: Sweden El-Kretsen SEK 1.3/kg NMC (about EUR 0.12, my conversion); France Ecosystem EUR 0.175/kg NMC; Latvia LZP EUR 0.230/kg (from 1 Jan 2026); Estonia EES-Ringlus EUR 0.29/kg; Denmark Batteriretur DKK 23.15/kg (about EUR 3.10, my conversion); Netherlands ARN EUR 25-130 per pack by weight band (EUR 55 for a 350-600 kg pack). The Latvian fee (EUR 0.23/kg, about EUR 92 for a 400 kg pack) is far below the real recycling price (EUR 1.31+/kg at GRS). It is what producers pay the scheme, not necessarily what the scheme pays a collector; whether LZP would pay a take-back/treatment fee to a Latvian hub is not found. (3) Black mass: no verifiable numeric 2026 EXW Europe NCM payable was found; Fastmarkets data is paywalled. The latest free Fastmarkets figures are 2024 (EXW Europe 47-53% in Jan 2024, 57.75% average in June 2024; Fastmarkets' own 2026 commentary says Europe keeps a structural discount to Asia, and EOL-origin material faces weaker demand due to hazardous-waste export restrictions). Fastmarkets' 2026 monthly updates say CIF South Korea payables hit records above 100% in early 2026, then black mass values fell across every region in September 2026. (4) The newest independent economics are negative for pure recycling: the HHL Leipzig/SAFELOOP study (Aug 2026) finds about EUR -1.90/kg of pack at market prices, with hazardous-goods transport about 16 times conventional freight; North American LFP gate fees are USD 1.50-2/kg (Benchmark, July 2026) while recyclers pay USD 2/kg or more for high-value chemistries. (5) No public tender with a per-kg or per-pack price for bus/fleet EV battery recycling was found. No published Riga-Helsinki, Riga-Tallinn or Riga-Poland ADR rate was found; the only road rates found are Warsaw-Duisburg EUR 1.45/km contract and 1.51/km spot (Q2 2026) and a 2020 Latvian truck operating cost of EUR 0.82/km. Implication for the 'cannot lose money' structure: never take a pack for free. Charge an inbound gate fee at least equal to the recycler's quote plus freight (about EUR 1.8-2/kg for undamaged NMC, EUR 4+/kg for LFP or damaged packs), or take only packs whose second-life sale value exceeds the recycler's quote, and get a binding written quote from the recycler before accepting each pack.

items.question: (2a) Black mass price assessments / payables by Fastmarkets, Benchmark, Argus, SMM in 2025-2026
items.answer: No numeric 2026 EXW Europe NCM payable could be retrieved: Fastmarkets, Benchmark and Argus data are paywalled, and I found no SMM or Mysteel black mass figure. (b) Fastmarkets monthly updates in 2026: March 2026, EOL-origin material, particularly from Europe, faces weaker demand amid hazardous-waste export restrictions; Europe trades below production scrap; around 80% of Europe's EOL batteries now come from energy storage, so LFP black mass supply is rising; CIF South Korea and SE Asia payables hit record levels incl. the first assessment above 100%. September 2026 update: Europe should retain a structural discount due to limited refining capacity and export restrictions. October 2026 update: black mass values fell across every major region in September. Fastmarkets' US black mass payables were suspended from 1 Sep 2026 after a US export ban (effective 27 Aug 2026) and resumed 14 Oct 2026. (c) Benchmark, 11 May 2026: NCM payables in ex-China Asia, North America and Europe at all-time highs, especially for production scrap (no figures; paywalled). (d) Historical Fastmarkets Europe figures (2024, not current): Jan 2024 deals 47-53% EXW for Ni and Co, inferred price USD 3,030/t; June 2024 average 57.75%, hazardous-waste NCM 55-60% EXW, inferred USD 3,482/t. (b) Ti/Upply/IRU European Road Freight Rate Benchmark: contract index 148.0 and spot index 146.8 in Q2 2026 (index values; contract +15.2 pts year on year); Q1 2026 contract 140.1, spot 132.3. (f) Rule constraints: damaged/defective packs need ADR special provision 376, packing instructions P908/P911, and ADR 2025 tightened rules for damaged Li-ion and Na-ion; recalled or defective batteries are forbidden for ordinary road transport. (g) Non-battery DHL UK surcharges 2026: GBP 255 non-stackable pallet and GBP 85 ADR load-exemption surcharge (not lithium-specific). My rough estimate, not sourced: Riga-Warsaw about 900 km at EUR 1.5/km is about EUR 1,350 per truck before ADR premium; a truck carries roughly 20-30 packs of 400 kg, so about EUR 50-70 per pack for full-truck loads, but part loads and ADR specialist carriers will cost much more. It describes free (unentgeltlich) take-back from GRS-connected producers and only refers to batterien.grs-pro.de/grs-entgelt-stb-ind-fzg for the paid tariff. The EUR 1.31/kg, 3.68/kg and pallet prices are in the separate PDF 'GRS-Entgelt-STB-IND-FZG' (4 pages, Stand 01.01.2026) linked from that page. Cite that document.

The GRS price is not a general market gate fee. It is the charge for a German Rücknahmestelle (collection point) that hands over batteries of producers who are not members of GRS's producer-responsibility scheme. For batteries of GRS member producers, take-back and recycling is free (page 1 of the Leistungsverzeichnis), with minimum pickup 90 kg (dealers/voluntary points) or 180 kg (public waste authorities/treatment plants). Whether a Latvian hub can contract for either route is not established; use it only as a ceiling/reference quote.

Researcher's '(1a) damaged transport-critical NMC EUR 3.06/kg + EUR 825 container' could not be re-read; the free-scheme document shows the safety container S as a EUR 3,000 deposit per piece. Do not budget EUR 825 without confirming.

GRS Paloxe one-time-use charge differs by case: EUR 40 for the undamaged GRS 600 l Paloxe, EUR 119 for the red damaged-battery Paloxe; delivery flat rate EUR 87.50 (up to 3). Also a EUR 89.95 per container surcharge for wrongly prepared containers. These were not in the summary.

ARN EUR 45/55 is per battery INCLUDING VAT; most other figures in the list are excl. VAT, so the 25-fold spread mixes bases. LZP and the French/Estonian/Swedish/Danish/Austrian rates are excl. VAT (SEK source does not state VAT).

The 'about 25-fold' spread compares per-kg producer fees (Sweden SEK 1.3 about EUR 0.12 vs Denmark DKK 23.15 about EUR 3.10). Both conversions are the researcher's own and should be labelled estimates; at 11 SEK/EUR and 7.46 DKK/EUR the numbers hold arithmetically.

The statement that the Latvian fee is 'far below the real recycling price' compares a producer compliance fee (paid per kg placed on market) with a recycler gate price; they are different things and the comparison does not show whether LZP would pay a hub.

HHL attribution: the EUR -1.90/kg is a modelled interim result (HHL Leipzig/SAFELOOP per ess-news and ingenieur.de), although one search summary credits RWTH PEM. Label it 'model estimate', not market data. The 'Bundestag 19th term EUR 500-1,500 per tonne' older figure was not re-verified.

Fastmarkets: since 22 April 2026 the Europe NCM payable assessments exclude NCA material from scope/name (search result). The researcher noted the moisture limit but not this exclusion, which matters because the hub's feedstock includes NCA.
missed: Legal basis not cited: Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 Art. 61 puts take-back of waste EV batteries on producers (and distributors for LMT/EV at retail), which is the legal reason a hub could be paid by producers/PROs rather than charging owners. This, and Latvian transposition (who may collect, licence/permit, waste-carrier registration, hazardous-waste classification, ADR), were not researched. I could not verify the article numbers because my search quota ran out.

Transboundary shipment rules (Waste Shipment Regulation, Basel/OECD notification for black mass and batteries to Finland/Poland) cost and lead-time were not covered, even though the plan ships black mass abroad; the Fastmarkets text itself flags hazardous-waste export restrictions as depressing EOL black mass demand.
GRS minimum pickup quantities (90 kg dealers, 180 kg waste authorities) and the 15 working-day pickup window; the plan should confirm any chosen recycler's minimum lot size.

No evidence found that any recycler or PRO pays a collector per pack; the only 'income' evidence is the 2024 black mass payables and the generic USD 2/kg statement, both outside a verified 2026 European transaction. A 'cannot lose money' structure therefore rests on gate fees and written recycler quotes, not on revenues.

Second-life value side is not in this angle, and second-life resale (ENGYcell) carries its own conformity/liability requirements (Battery Regulation repurposing: the repurposer becomes the producer) that affect the profitability claim.
Currency/VAT: no check of cross-border VAT treatment (reverse charge) for invoicing a German or Finnish recycler, which affects the net numbers.

findings.angle: C: buyers of tested packs (second life) and the Baltic market
findings.summary: Verdict: no published, verifiable price paid per kWh by any European second-life buyer was found, and real asking prices for used packs are high (Leaf 40 kWh pack EUR 5,000 ex-VAT = about EUR 125/kWh nameplate; Tesla modules about EUR 70-140/kWh asking, vendor-claimed). The only buyer-side price points are a Voltfang pitch-deck ratio (buys at 1/5 of new, per a search summary; the PDF itself returned 403) and one North American quote (second-life ~USD 30/kWh vs recycler ~USD 8/kWh, energy-storage.news; page returned 403, so quoted via search snippet only). New cells are very cheap (CATL LFP storage cell about USD 65/kWh, TrendForce EV LFP 0.41 RMB/Wh on 22 Oct 2026), so a second-life buyer has little room to pay much, and a no-loss structure cannot assume the 30% 'best packs' sell at a profit. Safest design for 'cannot lose money per pack': take packs on a paid-take-back or consignment basis (OEM/insurer/fleet pays a gate fee, or we pay nothing upfront), sell second-life only against a signed purchase order, and fall back to recycling revenue otherwise. ENGYcell: Riga software-first BESS/VPP startup (EUR 450k incl. EUR 250k Change Ventures pre-seed + EU grant, Mar 2025), reportedly uses repurposed Tesla batteries from OX Drive; its own website says nothing about second-life, volumes, customers or prices. No Baltic second-life pilots or grants specific to second-life were found; Estonian/Baltic research says uptake is blocked by governance (classification, liability, certification, insurers' fire concerns). Many searches returned vendor/blog material; all figures are labelled by source type.

items.question: (1) ENGYcell (Riga): does it buy/use second-life EV batteries, chemistry, volumes, customers, product prices, battery sourcing, grants
items.answer: ENGYcell (EngyCell) is a Riga energy-management startup: BESS hardware (utility/C&I), automated trading software and a VPP platform; software is the main focus. Not checked: LinkedIn, Lursoft/Firmas.lv financials, grant database (LIAA/CORDIS) records. Conclusion: plausible buyer of small numbers of Tesla-type modules, but no evidence it pays any price or buys at volume; must be asked directly.

findings.angle: D: Latvian and Baltic supply side and demand for battery testing
findings.summary: Latvia's EV fleet is still young and small (13,916 passenger EVs at end-2025, CSB official; 14,385 BEV cars at 1 Jan 2026 per a trade article citing CSDD), so the volume of retiring traction packs is tiny today. Latvia saw 3,505 used BEVs and about 1,646 new BEVs registered in 2025, so the pool is import-driven and dominated by used Teslas, VW ID and Audi e-tron. Latvia's 43 licensed ELV operators took in 17,999 end-of-life vehicles in 2024 (official LVGMC report), but that report does not split out EVs or traction packs. I found no Latvian dealer, importer, insurer or ELV statement on what happens to removed traction batteries, and no Latvian traction-battery recycler. Regional supply data is thin: Finland recycled 52 full-electric cars in 2024 (trade press), and Norway had at least 14% of end-of-life Li-ion batteries stockpiled in 2024 (peer-reviewed abstract). Battery health tests have a real, priced, but small market in Latvia: CellDrive (self-described official AVILOO partner) lists €95-130, EV Tesla Service lists €60-100, an SS.LV ad lists €95. Dealer-side willingness to pay is only documented by AVILOO's own survey (€550-1,100 price premium with a certificate; vendor study, 7 non-Baltic countries). Implication for a no-loss structure: pack supply must be treated as an optional, small flow of a few hundred per year at most in Latvia (my estimate), so fixed costs should be near zero and testing revenue (a priced service) is the only demonstrable cash stream today.

items.question: 2. Baltic neighbours and Nordic/Poland: counts of retired traction batteries per year and who collects them
items.answer: No country gives a clean annual count of retired traction packs. Norway: ABR (Autoretur Battery Recycling), set up by the importers' association BIL via Autoretur AS, was approved by the Environment Agency as an EPR scheme and took over on 1 Nov 2025, using Autoretur's nationwide logistics; it expects up to 50,000 used high-energy batteries per year by 2030 and over 100,000 by 2035 (electrive, 12 Aug 2025). A peer-reviewed study of the Norwegian system found at least 14% of end-of-life Li-ion batteries were stockpiled in 2024, due to a weak market for used batteries, mismatched price expectations and unclear responsibility for damaged batteries from insurance write-offs. Norway is the clearest warning that supply of used packs can exceed buyers. Finland: Suomen Autokierrazys (owned by the importers' group Autotuojat ja -teollisuus) runs the producer scheme for traction batteries; Moottori reported 52 full-electric cars recycled in 2024 versus 13 in 2023 (unverified source, trade press); Fortum Ikaalinen mechanical capacity is about 3,000 t/yr, roughly 10,000 EV packs (capacity, 2021 data). items.question: 3. What do Latvian dealers, importers, garages, insurers and ELV dismantlers do with removed traction batteries? Producer register / take-back information?
items.answer: No Latvian statement, press article, tender or interview found on the fate of removed traction batteries from Tesla service, Moller Baltic Import (VW group), Hyundai, Kia, Nissan, Renault, BMW, Mercedes, garages, insurers (BTA, Balta, Gjensidige, If) or ELV centres. Legal framework found: batteries producers and authorised representatives are registered in the battery producers registry under EU Regulation 2023/1542 article 56(3) (Latvijas Vestnesis 30 Apr 2026 amendment to Cabinet Regulation 331); producers or their contracted waste managers file market and collection/recycling reports; the Waste Management Law amendment text says producers fund collection and recycling of batteries including transport batteries. Lvportals (2023) says sorted batteries are sent to recyclers outside Latvia; a 2020 LSM piece mentions a stalled Eco Lead battery recycling plant project at Kalnciems with no current status. Moller Baltic Import's published VW warranty rules (2020, Lithuanian) do not mention traction batteries; a Latvian buyer's guide says many manufacturers' battery warranties hold down to 70-80% SOH. An LSM report (4 Feb 2025) says Latvian garages lack EV-trained mechanics and most Latgale services do not offer EV maintenance. An independent Riga firm, EV Tesla Service, repairs HV batteries at module and cell level and sells spare parts via an online shop, but its page does not say whether it buys defective packs. Practical next steps (not done, would need phone or e-mail): ask Moller, Hyundai/Kia and Nissan importers for their EPR scheme and battery take-back contact; ask the Latvian state environment service for the battery-producer register entries and the list of licensed hazardous-waste carriers.

items.question: 4a. Who offers EV battery health tests in Latvia and what do they charge?

CellDrive (celldrive.lv), self-described official AVILOO partner and distributor in Latvia, mobile service in Riga and surroundings: Auto Check EUR 50, EV Battery (SoH plus AVILOO CARA certificate) EUR 95 (booking form says EUR 120, inconsistent), Hybrid Check EUR 80, EV Pro EUR 130; claims 500+ tests; static AVILOO test takes 30-60 minutes; targets buyers, sellers, dealers and insurers (vendor page, copyright 2026). items.question: 4b. Is there demand, used-EV sales volume, dealer behaviour and any willingness-to-pay evidence?
items.answer: Volume exists and is growing fast: 3,505 used BEVs registered in Latvia in 2025 (Q4: 1,031) and 1,750 in H1 2026, about two-thirds of EV registrations, so about 3,500 or more potential test customers per year (my estimate; actual test uptake unknown). Upper bound on test revenue if every used import were tested once at EUR 95 would be about EUR 330k per year (my arithmetic); realistic capture is a small fraction, and no uptake rate for Latvia was found. Dealer behaviour: Latvian dealers and SIXT recommend a pre-purchase test but I found no data on how many dealers actually require one; in Estonia a used-car manager (ERR, Oct 2023) said buyers often doubt 3-5 year old batteries, while he considers fear exaggerated. Willingness to pay: the only study found is AVILOO's own 2024 remarketing survey (n=913, online, Van Westendorp, Germany, Austria, Belgium, France, UK, Norway, Sweden, June-July 2024, published 4 Mar 2025): buyers would pay at least EUR 550 to 1,100 more for a used EV with a battery test certificate. It is a vendor study with no Baltic sample, so it supports the concept, not the Latvian price. No Latvian, Lithuanian or Estonian WTP study found. Context from Latvian buyer guides: battery replacement can cost EUR 4,000 to over EUR 12,000 (Lithuanian guide; secondary), so a EUR 95 test is cheap insurance. Latvian state purchase aid for used BEVs (EUR 3,000, new BEV/PHEV EUR 4,000 reported Feb 2026) pushes used volumes up; one search result mentions a ministry discussion of a 12-month first-registration limit for used EVs in the aid rules (March 2026 document, outcome not seen), which is a risk to the used flow.

checks.note: LSM 21 Apr 2026 (a643911) reports a EUR 40m programme with EUR 3,000 to 9,000 per vehicle depending on type and Golden Family status. It adds EUR 2,000 for scrapping an old ICE car. Used cars must be at most 7 years old since first registration, at most 150,000 km, and registered in Latvia for no more than 12 months. The 12-month limit is therefore in the approved rules, not just discussed. The programme runs until funds are exhausted, at the latest 31 Dec 2029. The previous programme funded 6,467 purchases. This directly affects the used-import inflow and the age and km profile of future retired packs. The researcher's autopase.lv figures were not reconfirmed and should be dropped.

checks.note: likumi.lv shows an amendment to Cabinet Regulation 331, adopted 28 Apr 2026 (protocol 24, 11 §), published 30 Apr 2026 (OP 2026/83.1), in force 1 May 2026. It requires battery producers and authorised representatives to register in the battery producers registry under art. 56(3). The researcher gave the publication date but not the adoption or effect dates. The page says the amending act is MK noteikumi Nr. 227, and I did not check that the base regulation number 331 matches. Secondary law-firm summaries say EV-battery take-back by producers and distributors is free of charge under arts. 60-62 from 18 Aug 2025. I could not retrieve the EUR-Lex article text.

corrections: Latvian state EV aid is wrong or outdated in the findings. The EUR 4,000 new / EUR 3,000 used figures (autopase.lv) should be replaced by the approved scheme per LSM 21 Apr 2026: EUR 40m, EUR 3,000-9,000 per vehicle, used cars at most 7 years old, at most 150,000 km, registered in Latvia for no more than 12 months, EUR 2,000 scrapping bonus. The 12-month rule is enacted, not merely 'discussed'. The previous EUR 30m programme funded 6,467 purchases (LSM, same article).
Norway ABR forecast: the source says volumes will exceed 50,000 per year by about 2030 and more than 100,000 by 2035, not 'up to 50,000'. It is a forecast, not a count.
The Norwegian stockpile study is peer-reviewed academic literature (Transport Policy vol. 188, art. 104377), not 'official'. Only the 'at least 14%' lower bound is given.
Finnish 52 cars is attributed to the Suomen Autokierratys CEO (Moottori, 18 Jan 2025), so it is not 'unverified'. It counts vehicles, not packs, and is single-source.

Uzladets used/new BEV figures are credited to Eleport, not directly to CSDD. The Eleport total (1,646 new BEV = 7.2% share) differs from the EU AFO total (1,602 BEV, 22,506 cars). Treat 'about 3% difference' as a normal source discrepancy.

The CSB TRC012 table is titled 'registered electric vehicles' and carries no BEV/PHEV flag. Say 'registered electric vehicles (CSB definition not stated)' rather than 'BEV'. The CSB share is 1.73% of passenger cars at end-2025, which can anchor the fleet share.

CellDrive 'Auto Check EUR 50' is a fault-code check, not a battery test. Do not include it in battery-test price ranges. VAT treatment is unstated on all three Latvian price pages, so margin calculations must not assume net or gross.

The researcher's own estimate of 'low tens to low hundreds' of scrapped EVs per year in Latvia is unsourced. It stays an estimate. A rough bound from official data: 6,369 EVs in 2023 growing to 13,916 in 2025, with ELVs at about 18,000 per year, but no EV scrap rate exists. The 'few hundred packs per year' supply claim is likewise unsourced.

The LVGMC 'Akumulatori' 95.8 t is all ELV battery types (mostly lead-acid) and must not be read as traction-pack tonnage. The researcher said this correctly, but any downstream use must keep that caveat.
missed: The EUR 3,000-9,000 aid and the 12-month Latvian registration cap for used cars (LSM 21 Apr 2026) are the biggest demand-side change. They throttle the used-import flow into the subsidy, and they mean used imports registered more than 12 months earlier are outside it. Also, 6,467 purchases under the previous programme is a verified count of subsidised vehicles.

EU Battery Regulation 2023/1542 puts extended producer responsibility on producers, with free take-back of EV batteries from 18 Aug 2025 (law-firm summaries: HSF Kramer, Oct 2025, not the Official Journal text). For a start-up this is an inflow lever, because the legal obligation sits with producers or importers who must fund collection and recycling. It is also a cost risk, because Latvian collection and recycling may require producer or PRO registration or a waste carrier or treatment permit. The researcher did not check what permits a Latvian collector needs.

The researcher found no Latvian pack-grade price or buyer for second-life packs. The only cash stream is test fees, and that market is already contested by at least three providers using the same AVILOO kit, with a distributor selling the kit to competitors.

No evidence of any importer's EPR scheme or PRO contact in Latvia; the producer register entries have not been pulled. This is the key next step for supply and for any gate-fee or take-back payment, since the payment direction (recycler pays us, or we pay) is unknown.

Fleet-age context. Latvia's EV fleet more than doubled in two years, but the stock is mostly under 5 years old. Retirement volume is therefore tiny in 2026-2028, and the 'dozens to hundreds' estimate is not backed by any data point (the CSB data has no age split).

Not verified: Auto Asociacija H1 2025 figures (1,505 used EVs), the Lithuanian and Estonian figures, the German, Danish, Norwegian and Polish test-price benchmarks, the Tesla Riga pop-up, and the Moller/EV-service statements. I did not re-open these. Treat them as unconfirmed by this check.

checked_items.item: 1. Latvian permits for collecting, storing, sorting and shredding EV traction batteries
checked_items.answer: A third-party pack hub needs a State Environmental Service (VVD) waste management permit before collecting, sorting or storing waste (Waste Management Law s.12). The s.12(6) exemptions (retail household collection, battery collection points under Reg 2023/1542 Arts 59-60, a holder's own short-term storage) probably do not cover a commercial hub. This is a reading by the researcher and was not confirmed with VVD. Fees under Cabinet Reg 703 are small: EUR 120 per activity, EUR 180 for two, EUR 240 for three or more, and EUR 70 for an amendment. Reg 703 sets no fixed decision deadline for a new permit. A mechanical shredding line is a B-category pollution permit (Annex 1: items 5.14 EEE shredding up to 75 t/day, 5.13 hazardous storage up to 1 year and up to 50 t, 5.12 hazardous storage over 1 year). A B permit replaces the separate Reg 703 permit. Annex 1 names no lithium-pack or black-mass line, so the correct category (5.14, 5.1 or A) is not found. The skeptic flagged that the researcher's idea that an intact pack under waste code 16 06 05 is non-hazardous (which would keep the hub below the hazardous-waste thresholds) is unverified and must not be used to plan around B-category. Black mass is reportedly being added to the EU hazardous-waste list (trade press, unconfirmed). The B-permit fee of EUR 362.83 comes from an old search snippet and is not usable. B-permit timing is not found (old texts suggest about 60 to 90 days, unverified).
key_numbers: Reg 703 state fee: EUR 120 / 180 / 240 for one / two / three or more activities
Amendment fee EUR 70, decision in 10 working days
Trader/intermediary registration EUR 100, decided in 1 month
B category thresholds: 50 t hazardous storage up to 1 year; shredding up to 75 t/day
B-permit fee EUR 362.83: UNVERIFIED, old snippet, do not budget
VVD financial security for a transport-only permit EUR 10,000/yr, hazardous multiplier 2.5: 2020 presentation, needs checking (costs angle)
checked_items.what_it_means_for_us: Start with a Reg 703 collection/storage/sorting permit (EUR 120 to 240) and do NOT buy a shredder yet. Shredding triggers a B pollution permit with unknown cost and timing. Ask VVD in writing which category applies before any equipment spend.

checked_items.item: 2. Fire rules for lithium battery storage
checked_items.answer: No lithium-specific storage clause was found in Cabinet Reg 238 (Fire Safety Regulations, 19.04.2016). Coverage of the full text is fair but not complete, so absence is not proven. The page says Reg 238 loses force on 2 January 2027 and no successor was found. Only general or lead/alkali charging-room rules exist (separate ventilated rooms, 50% of extinguishers suitable for electrical equipment up to 1000 V). The building norm is LBN 201-15 (Reg 333 of 2015); LBN 201-10 is apparently superseded. Fire-compartment sizes in its Table 3 were not retrieved. Insurer requirements for battery storage in Latvia: not found. International insurers (TT Club, Sept 2026) want a fire-resistant dedicated area, early detection, sprinklers and quarantine of damaged stock, with no pricing. The VUGD statistic of 39 battery/accumulator fires in 2025 covers all batteries, not EV packs, and must not be used as an EV-pack fire rate.
key_numbers: Reg 238 loses force 2 Jan 2027; successor not found
At least 50% of extinguishers suitable for electrical equipment (cl.261)
VUGD: 39 battery/accumulator fires in 2025 (all battery types)
Li-ion type-90 storage cabinet EUR 7,000-11,000 (small cells/packs only, not 300-500 kg packs)
checked_items.what_it_means_for_us: Fire is the one cost that can wipe us out and no premium is known. Do not sign a lease or accept any pack until a broker has quoted cover and a fire-risk assessment is done. Keep stock to a minimum (take packs only against a scheduled onward pickup).

checked_items.answer: Waste Management Law Art.43 fines are in fine units of EUR 5 each (the unit value rests on one trade-press explainer, consistent with VVD's 2021 figures). Euro values below are the researcher's conversion. Handling without a permit: legal person EUR 250-2,800, natural person EUR 70-1,000. Breach of cross-border shipment rules: legal person EUR 300-4,000. Producer not registered: EUR 250-1,750. Waste accounting breach: EUR 250-1,250. The fines are small next to the cost of a fire, a revoked permit or a repatriated illegal shipment. Not found: Natural Resources Tax for batteries, EPR-specific fines, criminal liability, and fines under the EU shipment regulation.

Illegal shipment, legal person: 60-800 units = EUR 300-4,000
Unregistered producer: EUR 250-1,750
1 fine unit = EUR 5
checked_items.what_it_means_for_us: Fines are not the main legal risk. The real exposure is a mis-classified shipment being treated as illegal (return-shipment costs, lost load) and permit revocation. Budget for compliance work, not for fines.

checked_items.answer: Cabinet Reg 331 (version of 1 May 2026, amended by Reg 227 of 28.04.2026) runs the battery producer register. The register holder is the Latvian Electrotechnical and Electronics Industry Association and the controller is the Ministry of Climate and Energy. Battery producers register before offering batteries on the Latvian market, with EUR 42.69 at registration and EUR 42.69 per year (invoice by 1 Feb, due 28 Feb). The registrar decides in 10 working days. The deadline for foreign producers to appoint a representative (15 June 2026) is already past. Reg 331 sets no registration duty for collectors, repurposers or recyclers. A waste manager can report on behalf of a producer under a contract (cl.32). NOT verified: whether a repurposer that sells a repackaged pack counts as a 'producer' under Reg 2023/1542 (it may, which would add EPR registration, conformity and liability duties). Under Reg 2023/1542 Art.60-62, secondary law-firm sources say EV batteries must be taken back free of charge by producers/distributors from 18 Aug 2025 (not checked against EUR-Lex).

Registrar decision 10 working days
Free producer take-back of EV batteries from 18 Aug 2025 (secondary law-firm summaries)
checked_items.what_it_means_for_us: Our own registration cost is trivial. The legal point that matters commercially is that the producer is obliged to fund take-back, so the hub should sell collection and treatment as a service to producers/importers/their scheme (a paid contract), not rely on owners paying. Selling second-life packs may make us a 'producer' with extra duties; settle this with a lawyer before the first sale.

checked_items.item: 5. Used versus waste status for cross-border moves (Reg 2023/1542, Annex XIV, DIWASS)
checked_items.answer: A state-of-health test record alone does not make a pack 'used'. Annex XIV (read through a German-law mirror, single source, EUR-Lex text not obtained) requires for each shipment: an invoice/contract showing direct reuse and full functionality, per-battery test records, a holder declaration that nothing is waste, protective packing, a test record attached to the pack (ID, tester, date, results), and a transport document. Any missing item means the load is treated as waste and presumed an illegal shipment. The reference to Reg 1013/2006 is outdated: it is replaced by Reg 2024/1157 (most provisions from 21 May 2026), so the new cross-reference needs checking. Waste, shredded fractions and black mass ship as waste. Black mass classification (green list or notification) is not found; trade press (Recycling International, EUWID) reports it being classed as hazardous waste in the EU list, with no legal act confirmed. DIWASS: the researcher's claim that it is 'mandatory from 21 May 2026 for waste shipments' was contradicted. Sources show a phase-in: amber-list from 21 May 2026, green-list (Annex VII) from January 2027, and a transition to 31 Dec 2026 for some electronic duties. Latvia's DIWASS authority code LV01 (single source). Reg 2024/1157 rules on exports for recovery to non-OECD countries apply from 21 May 2027 (single source, ERA Malta).
key_numbers: DIWASS start 21 May 2026 (phased; green list from Jan 2027)
VVD notification-procedure fee EUR 142.29: purpose unconfirmed, not usable
VVD contact for shipments: ap@vvd.gov.lv (VVD guidance PDF)
sources: https://pl.andersen.com/en/newsletter/mandatory-diwass-system-for-cross-border-waste-shipments-from-may-21-2026/ (trade press; use the URL as returned by search)
checked_items.what_it_means_for_us: Treat every inbound pack as waste by default. Only a pack with the complete Annex XIV file may be sold as a product across a border (this is where the 30% second-life sale to Poland/Finland gets paperwork-heavy). Packs we cannot document go out as waste with a recycler who has the notification permit. Black mass to Finland/Poland is OECD/EU, so allowed, but expect hazardous-waste notification time and cost.

checked_items.item: 6. Who collects traction batteries in Latvia and the Baltics
checked_items.answer: No Latvian traction-battery recycler and no named Latvian collector were found; sorted batteries are sent abroad (lvportals 2023), and an Eco Lead plant at Kalnciems is stalled (LSM 2020, no current status). The Latvian compliance scheme with a published EV-battery tariff is SIA Latvijas Zalais punkts (LZP). Estonia has EES-Ringlus with a tariff. Lithuania: no tariff or collector found. Neighbouring benchmarks: Norway's importers' scheme ABR started on 1 Nov 2025 and forecasts more than 50,000 packs per year by about 2030 and over 100,000 by 2035; a peer-reviewed study found at least 14% of end-of-life Li-ion batteries stockpiled in Norway in 2024 (weak used-battery market, price-expectation mismatch, unclear responsibility for insurer write-offs). Finland: 52 full-electric cars recycled in 2024 (13 in 2023). Recycler capacity nearby: Fortum Ikaalinen about 3,000 t/yr (2021 figure, grant for 5,000 t/yr in 2023), AE Elemental Zawiercie up to 12,000 t/yr (opened Sept 2024). These are nameplate capacities, not proof they take third-party packs.

checked_items.item: 9. Demand and price for battery health tests in Latvia
checked_items.answer: Three Riga providers publish prices: CellDrive (self-described AVILOO partner) EV Battery check EUR 95 (booking form says EUR 120) and EV Pro EUR 130; EV Tesla Service EUR 60 / 75 / 100; an SS.LV ad (11 Oct 2026) EUR 95 with AVILOO certificate. VAT status is unstated on all. The 'Auto Check EUR 50' is a fault-code check and not a battery test. The SS.LV advertiser also sells AVILOO equipment and training, so competitors can enter easily. Regional prices: Germany TUV SUD/AVILOO about EUR 99-100 and DEKRA EUR 120 (2023); Poland PLN 300-550 (2026); Denmark FDM DKK 893-1,050. Willingness to pay: only a vendor study (AVILOO, n=913, seven non-Baltic countries, 2024) says buyers would pay at least EUR 550-1,100 more for a used EV with a certificate; no Baltic study exists. Upper bound if all used imports were tested once at EUR 95 is about EUR 330k per year (our arithmetic); the real uptake is unknown. Car-level SoH tests are not pack-level grading.

checked_items.item: 10. Does ENGYcell buy packs, and what does it pay?
checked_items.answer: ENGYcell is a Riga software-first BESS/VPP start-up. BeBeez (19 Mar 2025) reports EUR 450,000 total funding (EUR 250,000 Change Ventures pre-seed plus an unquantified EU grant). Founders came from OX Drive and say they use repurposed EV batteries including Tesla ones (claim: 30% electricity cost cut at OX Drive). Its website says nothing about second-life, volumes, customers or prices. PitchBook shows USD 266K raised (conflict). SIA Engycell Batteries exists (share capital EUR 2,800). No evidence that it pays any price or buys at volume. With EUR 450k total funding, its purchasing power is small.

checked_items.item: 11. Other second-life buyers and what they pay
checked_items.answer: No European second-life buyer publishes a purchase price per kWh. Voltfang (Aachen): a pitch deck reportedly says it buys EV batteries at about one fifth of the new price (ratio only, PDF not opened), but a Voltfang interview says it has no price advantage, takes large batches from carmakers, and now uses new/overproduction cells. Rebaba (Stockholm) raised USD 4.6M seed in Sept 2026; its planned 40 MWh/yr is its own production capacity, and the claim of Stena/OKQ8 partners was not supported by the cited source. Others (Fenecon, Connected Energy, Mobility House, Zenobe, Eco Stor, Betteries, etc.): no price. The only quantified buyer-vs-recycler point (USD 30/kWh second-life against USD 8/kWh recycler) is an unnamed North American source in an article that appears to date from 2024 (page 403); not usable as a current price. No Baltic second-life project, tender or grant was found. A 2026 RTU paper says Baltic uptake is blocked by governance (classification, liability, certification, insurers). New cells are cheap: CATL LFP storage cell about USD 65/kWh (not available to a Latvian buyer without a Chinese licence or broker) and EV LFP prismatic 0.41 RMB/Wh (TrendForce, 22 Oct 2026).
key_numbers: Voltfang buys at about 1/5 of new price (ratio, vendor deck)
North America USD 30/kWh vs USD 8/kWh: stale, unnamed source
CATL LFP storage cell about USD 65/kWh; TrendForce EV LFP 0.41 RMB/Wh and NCM 0.63 RMB/Wh
Rebaba seed SEK 44.1M / USD 4.6M (Sept 2026)
checked_items.what_it_means_for_us: There is no verified price to base the 30% second-life revenue on, and falling new-cell prices squeeze it. Sell second-life only against a signed purchase order with price per kWh, never on spec. Model the 30% share as zero-profit in the base case.

checked_items.item: 13. Take-back fees paid by producers and schemes per kg
checked_items.answer: Verified 2026 producer fee tariffs, all what producers pay their scheme and not what a scheme pays a collector: Latvia LZP EUR 0.230/kg excl. VAT from 1 Jan 2026 (letter 25.09.2025, hosted on a third-party server, table layout resolved by the skeptic); Estonia EES-Ringlus EUR 0.29/kg; Sweden El-Kretsen SEK 1.3/kg NMC/NCA, SEK 2.1/kg LFP (about EUR 0.12 and 0.19, our conversion at 11 SEK/EUR); France Ecosystem EUR 0.175/kg NMC, 0.085 LFP excl. VAT (column assignment inferred); Austria Interzero EUR 0.20/kg; Denmark Batteriretur DKK 23.15/kg (about EUR 3.10, our conversion); Netherlands ARN EUR 55 per pack of 350-600 kg including VAT (about EUR 0.11-0.14/kg). Bases differ (ARN includes VAT). Lithuania, Norway, Finland, Belgium (no uniform price) not found. Whether LZP or any scheme pays a collector per kg is not found. These fees are far below the recycler price (item 14), so the schemes cannot fund treatment from producer fees at these levels unless they are paid recycler rebates we cannot see.
key_numbers: Latvia LZP EUR 0.230/kg (about EUR 92 per 400 kg pack)
Estonia EUR 0.29/kg
Denmark DKK 23.15/kg (about EUR 3.10)
Sweden SEK 1.3/kg NMC (about EUR 0.12)
Netherlands EUR 55 per 350-600 kg pack incl. VAT
checked_items.what_it_means_for_us: Do not assume the Latvian scheme will pay us EUR 0.23/kg or anything; that is a fee flowing to the scheme. The hub's income per pack must come from a negotiated service fee from the producer or importer. Compare: the cheapest realistic recycler cost is several times the Latvian producer fee.

checked_items.answer: No recycler publishes a gate-fee table (Fortum, Stena, Umicore, Hydrovolt, Eneris, AE Elemental and others searched, none found). The best real price is the GRS Service GmbH (Germany) tariff 'GRS-Entgelt-STB-IND-FZG', valid 1 Jan 2026, excl. VAT. It is what a German collection point pays to hand over batteries of producers who are not GRS members, so use it only as a reference ceiling. Undamaged NMC/NCA modules EUR 1.31/kg (cells 1.38); LFP/LMO modules EUR 3.68/kg (cells 3.93); first pallet slot EUR 214.50, each further slot EUR 125. Damaged but transport-safe: NMC modules EUR 1.44/kg, LFP EUR 4.38/kg; first slot EUR 236.50, further EUR 145. Damaged and transport-critical NMC modules EUR 3.06/kg plus a EUR 825 safety container: the skeptic could not read that page and the free-scheme document shows the container as a EUR 3,000 deposit, so do not budget the 825. The headline GRS number was cited to the wrong PDF in the findings; use the 'GRS-Entgelt-STB-IND-FZG' PDF. A 400 kg undamaged NMC pack costs about EUR 738 (400 x 1.31 + 214.50), about EUR 1.85/kg (our arithmetic). Market context: HHL Leipzig/SAFELOOP interim model (Aug 2026) shows about EUR -1.90/kg of pack at market prices (a model estimate, not market data); RWTH Aachen (2025) says European EV-battery recycling is unprofitable with transport up to 70% of cost; Benchmark via NPR (13 Jul 2026) says North American LFP gate fees are USD 1.50-2/kg while recyclers pay USD 2/kg or more for valuable chemistries. Black mass: no numeric 2026 European payable found (paywalled). Last free figures are 2024: EXW Europe NCM about 55.8% (May) and 57.75% (June) of nickel/cobalt. Fastmarkets says Europe keeps a structural discount, end-of-life black mass faces weak demand, values fell in all regions in September 2026, and since 22 April 2026 the Europe NCM assessment excludes NCA.
key_numbers: GRS undamaged NMC/NCA modules EUR 1.31/kg excl. VAT; LFP modules EUR 3.68/kg
GRS first pallet EUR 214.50, further EUR 125
400 kg NMC pack about EUR 738 (about EUR 1.85/kg), our arithmetic
HHL model: about EUR -1.90/kg of pack; transport 16 times conventional freight
US LFP gate fee USD 1.50-2/kg; one Tesla pack quoted -USD 1,800 to a salvage yard
EXW Europe NCM black mass 57.75% in June 2024 (no 2026 figure)
checked_items.what_it_means_for_us: This is the core of 'cannot lose money': the cost of getting rid of a pack is positive (about EUR 1.3-1.9/kg for NMC, EUR 3.7-4.4/kg for LFP or damaged), not a payment to us. Our own mechanical process plus black-mass export is unproven and, per the HHL and RWTH studies, likely loss-making for a small player. The only safe rule: never accept a pack without a fee at least equal to a binding written recycler quote plus freight plus ADR plus margin.

checked_items.answer: No published Riga-Helsinki, Riga-Tallinn, Riga-Poland or lithium-pallet ADR rate was found, and no public tender with a per-kg price for bus or fleet batteries (searched English, Latvian, Finnish). Real price points: GRS logistics (above). Road freight benchmarks (Ti/Upply/IRU Q2 2026): contract index 148.0, spot 146.8; Warsaw-Duisburg EUR 1.45/km contract, EUR 1.51/km spot. A 2020 CNR figure puts the operating cost of a Latvian international truck at EUR 0.82/km (cost, not price). Our own unsourced estimate: Riga-Warsaw about 900 km at EUR 1.5/km is about EUR 1,350 per truck, so EUR 50-70 per pack for a full 20-30-pack truck before the ADR premium; part loads and ADR specialists cost far more. Damaged or defective packs need ADR special provision 376 and packing instructions P908/P911, and recalled or defective packs cannot go by ordinary road transport. HHL says hazardous-goods end-of-life battery transport averages 16 times conventional freight.
key_numbers: Warsaw-Duisburg EUR 1.45/km contract, EUR 1.51/km spot (Q2 2026)
Latvian truck operating cost EUR 0.82/km (2020)
Our estimate: EUR 50-70/pack full truck Riga-Warsaw before ADR premium (unsourced)
GRS pallet logistics EUR 214.50 / 125 per slot
checked_items.what_it_means_for_us: Freight is likely the largest controllable cost. The full-truck estimate only works with a pooled, scheduled load, which our early volume will not reach. Price each pack including a part-load ADR quote and carry freight as a pass-through to the customer.

checked_items.answer: Rent (asking, excl. VAT): Riga industrial about EUR 3.75-6.5/m2/month; Teika 876.6 m2 listing EUR 4,242/month (about EUR 4.84/m2, business.gov.lv, 16 Jun 2026); Colliers prime EUR 4.2-5.5 (snippet only, 2026 table header may be stale). Our estimate: 500 m2 at EUR 5/m2 is about EUR 2,500/month plus VAT and utilities, before any premium for fire-separated space (unquantified). Labour: average gross wage EUR 1,815 (2025), EUR 1,886 (Q2 2026); employer social tax 23.59% (employee 10.5%); minimum wage EUR 780. Our arithmetic: about EUR 2,331/month loaded per average FTE. Insurance: not found (no premium, rate or quote; TT Club and Lloyd's notes say cover may be hard to get). ADR safety adviser, waste-carrier fees, adviser day rates: not found (legal basis Cabinet Reg 156 and Reg 703). Test equipment: Fluke 1535 about EUR 1,834 excl. VAT; FLIR C5 about EUR 629, FLIR T560 EUR 20,249; pack cyclers and EIS meters not found (quote only). Fire equipment: type-90 Li-ion cabinets EUR 7,000-11,000 (cells and small packs only); fire-rated containers not priced. Plant comparables: Redux Bremerhaven about EUR 3M for a 10,000 t/yr line (2018), Fortum Ikaalinen EUR 4.5M grant (2023, total cost not stated), Primobius 50 tpd spoke USD 103.9M (engineering study, different scale). This part of the findings was not independently re-checked by a skeptic, and the fire-safety item was cut off in the source text.

Loaded cost per average FTE about EUR 2,331/month (our arithmetic)
Fluke 1535 about EUR 1,834 excl. VAT

Redux line about EUR 3M for 10,000 t/yr (2018)

Avoid owning a shredder (seven-figure risk); rent a small space or use a partner's site, and subcontract ADR transport and the safety adviser.

Voltfang buys at about 1/5 of the new price (investor-deck ratio, 2024; no EUR/kWh). North America USD 30/kWh second-life vs USD 8/kWh recycler: stale, unnamed source.

Not found: Alibaba B/C-grade LFP module prices; Kona, e-Golf, ID.3, Zoe, i3 pack listings; any European transaction price paid by a second-life buyer.
testing_prices: Latvia: CellDrive EV Battery (SoH + AVILOO certificate) EUR 95 (booking form EUR 120), EV Pro EUR 130; EV Tesla Service EUR 60 / 75 / 100; SS.LV ad 11 Oct 2026 EUR 95. VAT treatment unstated.

Regional: Germany TUV SUD/AVILOO about EUR 99-100, DEKRA EUR 120 (2023); AVILOO Flash EUR 79 / Premium EUR 99 (ADAC); Finland AVILOO Premium EUR 129; Norway NAF NOK 1,149 member / NOK 1,349 non-member; Denmark FDM DKK 893-1,050 and Premium DKK 2,295; Poland PLN 300-550, average PLN 427 (June 2026).

B-category pollution permit fee: EUR 362.83 issue / EUR 249.00 review from an old search snippet only; UNVERIFIED, not for budgeting. Timing not found.
Battery producer register (Reg 331): EUR 42.69 at registration and EUR 42.69 per year.
Transport-only waste permit: financial security EUR 10,000/yr, hazardous multiplier 2.5 (2020 VVD presentation, old, verify). VVD EUR 142.29 shipment-related fee: purpose unconfirmed.
Fines (our conversion at EUR 5/unit): permit-less handling EUR 250-2,800 (legal person); illegal shipment EUR 300-4,000.
ADR safety adviser course, exam and outsourced adviser fees, waste-carrier permit fee, insurance premium, lawyer fees: not found.

Hub running costs: Riga industrial rent EUR 3.75-6.5/m2/month (asking, excl. VAT); average gross wage EUR 1,886 (Q2 2026), employer social tax 23.59%, about EUR 2,331/month per average FTE loaded (our arithmetic); Li-ion type-90 cabinet EUR 7,000-11,000; Redux 10,000 t/yr line about EUR 3M (2018).

risks_that_remain: No source supports a guarantee that the hub 'cannot lose money'. The verified cost of disposing of an undamaged NMC pack at the one public tariff is about EUR 1.85/kg (about EUR 740 per 400 kg pack), while the Latvian producer fee is EUR 0.23/kg (about EUR 92). Profit exists only if a producer, importer or insurer signs a service fee that covers recycler quote plus freight plus ADR plus overhead plus margin. No such payer has been found.

Take only fee-covered packs: the structural rule is to accept a pack only after a signed fee at least equal to a binding recycler quote plus freight plus ADR plus fixed-cost share plus margin. Free or speculative intake breaks the 'cannot lose' premise. LFP and damaged packs cost EUR 3.7-4.9/kg at GRS, so they need a much higher fee or must be refused.

The 30% second-life revenue is unsupported: no verified European purchase price per kWh; Voltfang is moving to new cells and OEM batches; ENGYcell's funding is EUR 450k; new LFP cells cost about USD 65/kWh. Treat this share as zero profit until a signed purchase order exists.

Own mechanical processing (copper, aluminium, steel, black mass) has no verified revenue data and a likely negative margin at small scale (HHL model about -EUR 1.90/kg; RWTH: unprofitable). It needs a B pollution permit of unknown cost and timing and carries a seven-figure equipment risk (Redux about EUR 3M).

Fire: no Latvian lithium-specific rule found, but insurers may refuse or price cover prohibitively; no premium is known; one fire could end the company. Reg 238 loses force 2 Jan 2027 with no successor found.

Legal status of a pack: missing one Annex XIV item turns a 'used' export into a presumed illegal waste shipment. Becoming a repurposer may make us a 'producer' under Reg 2023/1542. Black mass may be hazardous waste with notification duties; Reg 1013/2006 references are being replaced by Reg 2024/1157, and DIWASS has a phased start.

Supply risk: Latvia has about 14k EVs, a young fleet, and no scrap statistics; the 'few hundred packs per year' guess is unsourced. Norway shows stockpiling when buyers lag. The enacted 12-month registration cap on subsidised used imports may slow the used flow.

Competition for supply: producers' schemes (LZP and others) and the recycler's own take-back route (free for scheme members at GRS) may bypass us. Importers may already have contracts with foreign recyclers.
Testing is a thin market: three Riga providers already on the same AVILOO kit at EUR 60-130, and the equipment is for sale to competitors. VAT status of those prices is unknown.

Data quality: several figures are single-source or vendor claims (Voltfang 1/5, CommodityForge, bms-ev.com, evshop, Colliers snippet, LV01 code, EUR-Lex texts read via a German mirror). Fee conversions (SEK, DKK, fine units) are our own estimates. The costs-angle fire-safety item was truncated in the source text and the costs angle has no independent skeptic check.
Black mass price is unknown for 2026 and fell in Sept 2026; revenue from black mass cannot be modelled from verified European data.
Currency, VAT and reverse-charge treatment for invoices to foreign recyclers were not researched.
still_needs_a_human: Binding written quotes per pack (NMC, LFP, damaged, transport-critical), minimum lot, pickup rules and notification handling for Latvian-origin packs: ask Fortum (Finland), AE Elemental (Zawiercie), Eneris, Stena Recycling, GRS Service GmbH, plus any other recycler we consider. Ask each for a price per kg for packs and for black mass, and who arranges ADR transport.

Will importers/producers pay a collector, and how much per pack: call Moller Baltic Import (VW group), Hyundai and Kia, Nissan, Renault, BMW and Mercedes importers, Tesla Latvia (pop-up opened Aug 2026), and Latvijas Zalais punkts. Ask: who is your registered producer rep, what is your battery take-back contract today, and what do you pay per kg or per pack? Pull the battery producer register entries (Latvian Electrotechnical and Electronics Industry Association / Ministry of Climate and Energy).

Letter of intent from ENGYcell and at least one other buyer (Voltfang, Fenecon, Rebaba, a Baltic utility or telecom) stating chemistry, volume, price per kWh, payment and liability terms: contact ENGYcell directly.

Which VVD permit category applies to storing, testing, dismantling, and later shredding lithium packs (Reg 703 permit, B pollution permit, hazardous-waste thresholds), expected processing time and the current B-permit fee; whether an intact pack is hazardous (code 16 06 05 vs 16 06 01/02/03/06): Valsts vides dienests (VVD) permits department and ap@vvd.gov.lv for shipments.

Whether a repurposer/graded-pack seller is a 'producer' under Reg 2023/1542 (registration under Reg 331, EPR, conformity, battery passport from 18 Feb 2027): Ministry of Climate and Energy (VARAM) and a Latvian environmental/EU battery-regulation lawyer. Also have the lawyer verify Annex XIV against the EUR-Lex text, the new Reg 2024/1157 cross-references, black mass classification and the DIWASS timetable.

Fire and insurance: a broker quote (for example Marsh, Aon, BTA, Balta, Gjensidige, or a specialist/Lloyd's route) for hazardous-waste/lithium storage; a VUGD (State Fire and Rescue Service) opinion on the planned site and whether a successor to Reg 238 is planned; a fire-risk assessment of the chosen building and LBN 201-15 compartment limits.

Freight: quotes for ADR class 9 lithium pallets and part loads Riga to Helsinki/Tallinn/Poland from at least three ADR carriers (for example Latvian and Polish hazardous-goods hauliers), including damaged-pack surcharges (special provision 376, P908/P911); the cost of an outsourced ADR safety adviser and the VVD waste-carrier permit conditions.
Landlord quotes for fire-separated warehouse space, including utilities and VAT: Colliers Latvia or direct landlords (e.g. the Teika and Imanta listings).

Equipment quotes for a pack cycler, EIS and fire-safe test enclosure (Digatron, Bitrode, Chroma, EA, Aviloo/partner): only vendors can give prices. Ask CellDrive/AVILOO whether we can partner instead of competing on tests.

Tender and customer data: ask Riga's Rigas satiksme, Daugavpils and Liepaja bus operators what their bus makers' take-back clauses say and what they were quoted; search TED/EIS (Latvia) for CPV 90500000 and 'akumulatori' (not done).
Accountant: VAT/reverse charge on cross-border invoices to recyclers and the tax treatment of take-back fees; check Latvian Natural Resources Tax for batteries.
Funding check: whether any Norway Grants/LIAA, LVIF, CINEA or EIT Urban Mobility call exists for second-life or take-back pilots (programme sites were not fetched, so absence is not proven).
